Two conditions have to be written down and then combined.
**Condition 1 — the de Broglie relation.**
λ = h / (mv)
**Condition 2 — what the question states.** The wavelength equals the distance the electron
travels in one second, and distance = speed × time = v × 1 s, so
λ = v
**Combine them.**
v = h / (mv)
v² = h / m
**v = √(h/m)** ✓
So the speed is the square root of Planck's constant divided by the electron's mass.
The distractors are the same symbols shuffled: √(m/h) is the reciprocal, √(h/p) confuses mass
with momentum, and √(h/2KE) comes from a different relation altogether.
A quick dimensional check confirms (b): [h] = kg m² s⁻¹ and [m] = kg, so h/m has units
m² s⁻², and its square root is **m s⁻¹** ✓ a speed.
Out of curiosity, the number is tiny: √(6·626 × 10⁻³⁴ / 9·11 × 10⁻³¹) = √(7·27 × 10⁻⁴) ≈
**0·027 m s⁻¹** — under three centimetres a second, which for an electron is almost
stationary. Its de Broglie wavelength would then be 2·7 cm, enormous on an atomic scale, and
that is exactly why the two can be made equal.
∴ √(h/m).
pradeep|Chemistry|0|37|Pradeep Chemistry:
Orbital angular momentum is
**L = √(l(l + 1)) ħ**
so L = 0 requires **l = 0**, and l = 0 means an **s** orbital.
Among the options:
**(a) 2s** — l = **0** ⇒ L = √(0 × 1) ħ = **0** ✓
(b) 2p — l = 1 ⇒ L = √2 ħ ✗
(c) 3d — l = 2 ⇒ L = √6 ħ ✗
(d) 4f — l = 3 ⇒ L = √12 ħ ✗
So the electron may be in a **2s** orbital.
The zero is not an accident of the formula; it has a clear physical meaning. An **s orbital is
spherically symmetrical**, the same in every direction, so there is no axis about which
anything could be said to circulate. With no preferred direction, there is no angular
momentum.
This is also where **Bohr's model fails**. Bohr assumed L = nh/2π, which for n = 1 gives ħ,
not zero — he pictured the electron going round the nucleus like a planet. Quantum mechanics
says the 1s and 2s electrons have **no** orbital angular momentum at all, and experiment
agrees. It is one of the clearest demonstrations that orbits had to give way to orbitals.
Note the principal quantum number is irrelevant here: 1s, 2s, 3s and 4s all have L = 0.
∴ 2s.

'Zero electron density in the xy plane' means the xy plane is a **nodal plane** — a surface
where the wavefunction vanishes.
Take each orbital and ask where its lobes point.
**(c) p_z** ✓ The two lobes lie along the **z axis**, one above the xy plane and one below,
with opposite phase. Between them the wavefunction must pass through zero, and it does so
over the whole **xy plane**. That plane is therefore a node, with **zero** electron density ✓
**(d) d_xy** ✗ Its four lobes lie **in** the xy plane itself, between the x and y axes, so
that plane carries the **maximum** density — the exact opposite. Its nodal planes are xz and
yz.
**(b) d_x²−y²** ✗ Also has its lobes **in** the xy plane, along the x and y axes.
**(a) d_z²** ✗ Has two lobes along z and a **doughnut** of electron density encircling the
nucleus in the xy plane, so the density there is not zero either. (Its nodes are two cones,
not planes.)
So only p_z is empty in the xy plane.
The general rule: a p orbital has **one** nodal plane, perpendicular to its own axis, so p_x
is empty in the yz plane and p_y in the xz plane. Most d orbitals have **two** nodal planes.
∴ p_z.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|40|Pradeep Chemistry:
The number of **radial** (spherical) nodes is
**radial nodes = n − l − 1**
and it is worth keeping the three counts straight:
radial nodes = n − l − 1
angular nodes = l
**total** nodes = n − 1
**For 3s:** n = 3, l = 0
radial nodes = 3 − 0 − 1 = **2** ✓
**For 2p:** n = 2, l = 1
radial nodes = 2 − 1 − 1 = **0** ✓
So the answer is **2 and 0** — option (a).
The 2p orbital having **no** radial node is the point worth noticing. It still has **one**
node — the angular one, the nodal plane through the nucleus — so its total node count is
n − 1 = 1, as it must be. But there is no spherical shell of zero density within it.
The 3s orbital, by contrast, has no angular nodes at all (it is spherical), so all of its
n − 1 = 2 nodes are radial: two concentric spherical surfaces where the electron is never
found.
Option (d), 2 and 1, is what you get by counting the 2p orbital's **angular** node as a
radial one, which is the usual mistake.
∴ 2 and 0.

Picture the five d orbitals.
**d_xy, d_yz, d_xz** — each has **four lobes** lying between a pair of axes: d_xy between the
x and y axes, and so on. Apart from their orientation in space they are identical
cloverleaves.
**d_x²−y²** — also has **four lobes**, but they lie **along** the x and y axes rather than
between them. In shape it is the same cloverleaf, merely rotated by 45°.
**d_z²** — the odd one out. It has **two lobes** along the z axis plus a **ring (torus)** of
electron density around the middle in the xy plane. That is a different shape altogether,
not a cloverleaf at all.
So the first **four** have the same shape and only the fifth differs ✓ — option (c).
The reason is that there are only **five** independent d functions, but the natural way to
write them suggests six: d_xy, d_yz, d_xz, d_x²−y², d_y²−z² and d_z²−x². The last two are not
independent, and the combination that survives is written d_z², which is really
d_(2z²−x²−y²) — hence its unusual shape with the collar.
Despite looking different, all five are **degenerate** in a free atom: they have exactly the
same energy. Only when ligands approach, as in a complex, does the difference in shape split
them into t₂g and e_g sets.
∴ the shapes of the first four orbitals are similar but that of the fifth orbital is
different.

Confirm first that the three really are isoelectronic:
Ar : Z = 18, neutral ⇒ **18 electrons**
K⁺ : Z = 19, lost one ⇒ 19 − 1 = **18**
Ca²⁺ : Z = 20, lost two ⇒ 20 − 2 = **18** ✓
With the same eighteen electrons occupying the same shells, the size is decided by **nuclear
charge alone**. More protons pull the same cloud in tighter, so the species with the highest
Z is the smallest.
Ordering by atomic number: Ca (20) > K (19) > Ar (18)
so the radii run the other way, and in **increasing** order:
**Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < Ar** ✓
The measured values bear it out: Ca²⁺ 99 pm, K⁺ 133 pm, Ar 154 pm (van der Waals).
The quick rule for any isoelectronic set: arrange by **charge**, from most positive to most
negative, and that is the order of increasing size. Here 2+, 1+, 0 gives the answer directly
without looking anything up.
Notice how large the effect is — two extra protons shrink the species by more than a third.
The same reasoning extended to anions would continue Ar < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < P³⁻, since each added
electron with no extra proton swells the cloud further.
∴ Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < Ar.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|53|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The condition 'the highest principal quantum number is **4**' means the atom uses shells 1
to 4 and **no** shell beyond. That restriction, combined with the Aufbau filling order, is
what limits the answer.
**Which subshells can be filled?** The order of filling is
1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, **4s**, 3d, **4p**, then **5s**, then 4d, then 5p, 6s, 4f …
The 4d and 4f subshells, although they belong to n = 4, are only filled **after 5s** — and an
electron in 5s would make the highest principal quantum number **5**, which the question
forbids. So 4d and 4f are out of reach.
**Count what is left:**
1s² = 2
2s² 2p⁶ = 8
3s² 3p⁶ = 8
4s² = 2
3d¹⁰ = 10
4p⁶ = 6
total = **36 electrons** ✓
That is **krypton**, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁶ — the last element whose highest
occupied shell is the fourth.
The trap is to answer **32**, the full capacity 2n² of the fourth shell, or to add up every
subshell with n ≤ 4 and get 60. Both ignore that the Aufbau order, not the shell capacity,
decides what an atom can actually hold.
∴ 36.

Note: the printed key gives (b), 18. Eighteen electrons would be argon, whose highest
principal quantum number is 3, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (c).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|63|Pradeep Chemistry:
The de Broglie relation is
**λ = h / (mv)**
With the velocity the **same** for all four, λ depends only on the mass, and **inversely**:
the lightest particle has the longest wavelength.
Compare the masses:
CO₂ molecule — 44 u
NH₃ molecule — 17 u
proton — 1 u
**electron — 1/1836 u ≈ 0·00055 u** ✓ by far the lightest
So the **electron** has the largest de Broglie wavelength ✓
The margin is enormous: the electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton and some
80 000 times lighter than a CO₂ molecule, so at equal speeds its wavelength is 80 000 times
longer.
This is exactly why **wave behaviour is observable for electrons and not for molecules**. An
electron accelerated through a modest voltage has a wavelength of around 10⁻¹⁰ m — comparable
to the spacing between atoms in a crystal — so it diffracts, and electron diffraction became
a standard tool for determining structures. The Davisson–Germer experiment, which confirmed
de Broglie's hypothesis, worked for precisely this reason.
A molecule of CO₂ at the same speed would have a wavelength far too short for any lattice to
diffract.
∴ electron.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|6|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Write the configuration of each ion, remembering that a transition metal loses its **4s**
electrons **before** any 3d electron, then count the unpaired electrons by Hund's rule.
**(a) Cu²⁺** — Cu is Z = 29, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Removing two electrons gives [Ar] **3d⁹**:
four orbitals paired and one holding a single electron ⇒ **1 unpaired**
**(c) Ni²⁺** — Ni is Z = 28, [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². Removing the two 4s gives [Ar] **3d⁸**:
three pairs and two singles ⇒ **2 unpaired**
**(b) Cr³⁺** — Cr is Z = 24, [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. Removing three gives [Ar] **3d³**:
one electron in each of three orbitals ⇒ **3 unpaired**
**(d) Fe³⁺** — Fe is Z = 26, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Removing the two 4s and one 3d gives [Ar] **3d⁵**:
one electron in **each** of the five d orbitals, all spins parallel ⇒ **5 unpaired** ✓
So Fe³⁺ has the most, with five.
The **half-filled 3d⁵** configuration is the reason, and it is why Fe³⁺ is so stable and so
readily formed from Fe²⁺ in air. It also makes Fe³⁺ the most strongly paramagnetic of the
four, with a magnetic moment of √(5 × 7) = 5·92 Bohr magnetons.
The step that must not be skipped is removing the **4s electrons first**: taking them from
3d instead would give Fe³⁺ as 3d⁸ and the wrong count entirely.
∴ Fe³⁺.

Note: the printed key gives (c), Ni²⁺, which is 3d⁸ with only two unpaired electrons. Fe³⁺
is 3d⁵ with five, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|27|Pradeep Chemistry:
The question asks which item carries **both** descriptions of light at once.
**(a) Interference** and **(c) Diffraction** — both are **purely wave** phenomena. They occur
because waves superpose, and no particle picture explains them. Neither mentions particles ✗
**(b) E = mc²** — Einstein's mass-energy relation. It treats the photon purely as something
with **mass-equivalent energy**, a **particle** statement, with no wave quantity in it ✗
**(d) E = hν** ✓ — this single equation contains **both** natures:
**E**, the energy of one photon, is a **particle** property — it is the energy carried by a
single indivisible packet
**ν**, the frequency, is a **wave** property — only something that oscillates has a frequency
The equation says the energy of the particle is fixed by the frequency of the wave, so the
two descriptions are bound together in one expression. That is precisely what **wave-particle
duality** means.
The same point can be made with the de Broglie relation λ = h/p, which links a wave property
(wavelength) to a particle property (momentum). In both, **Planck's constant h is the bridge**
between the two pictures — which is why h appears wherever quantum behaviour does.
∴ E = hν.

Apply the de Broglie relation, taking care with the units of mass.
**λ = h / (mv)**
**Step 1 — convert the mass to kilograms.**
10 g = **0·010 kg**
**Step 2 — compute the momentum.**
mv = 0·010 × 10 = **0·1 kg m s⁻¹**
**Step 3 — divide.**
λ = 6·626 × 10⁻³⁴ / 0·1
= **6·626 × 10⁻³³ m** ✓
The gram-to-kilogram conversion is the whole question: using 10 g directly gives
6·626 × 10⁻³⁶ m, which is option (d) and sits there waiting for exactly that slip.
The answer is worth pausing on. A wavelength of 10⁻³³ metres is about **10¹⁸ times smaller
than an atomic nucleus** — unimaginably far below anything that could ever be measured. This
is why a cricket ball shows no wave behaviour whatever: its wavelength is so short that
diffraction and interference are utterly undetectable.
Compare an **electron** at the same speed: with a mass of 9·11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, its wavelength
would be about 7 × 10⁻⁵ m, larger than many objects it meets — which is why electron
diffraction is routine and ball diffraction is not.
Mass is what separates the quantum world from the everyday one, and this calculation shows
it in a single number.
∴ 6·626 × 10⁻³³ m.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle is
**Δx · Δp ≥ h / 4π**
Look carefully at what appears in it: **position and momentum only**. The **mass does not
appear at all**.
So the minimum uncertainty in momentum depends solely on how precisely the position is known:
Δp ≥ h / (4π Δx)
Both the electron and the helium atom have their positions known within the **same** 1·0 nm,
so both have the **same** minimum uncertainty in momentum ✓
The electron's is given as 5·0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg m s⁻¹, so the helium atom's is
**5·0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg m s⁻¹** ✓ — option (b).
The question is really testing whether the mass is thought to matter, and the distractors are
scaled versions of the electron's value, as if it had to be multiplied by some mass ratio.
It does not.
Where the mass **does** enter is in the uncertainty in **velocity**: since Δp = m Δv,
Δv = Δp/m, and the helium atom is some 7300 times heavier than the electron, so its velocity
is pinned down 7300 times more precisely for the same Δp. That is why uncertainty is
negligible for heavy particles and dominant for electrons — but the momentum uncertainty
itself is identical.
∴ 5·0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg m s⁻¹.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|30|Pradeep Chemistry:
Start from Heisenberg's principle in the form that gives the velocity:
Δx · m Δv ≥ h / 4π
**Δv = h / (4π m Δx)**
**Step 1 — convert the distance.**
0·1 Å = 0·1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = **1 × 10⁻¹¹ m**
**Step 2 — the denominator.**
4π m Δx = 4 × 3·1416 × 9·11 × 10⁻³¹ × 1 × 10⁻¹¹
= 12·566 × 9·11 × 10⁻⁴²
= **1·145 × 10⁻⁴⁰**
**Step 3 — divide.**
Δv = 6·626 × 10⁻³⁴ / 1·145 × 10⁻⁴⁰
= **5·79 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹** ✓
The ångström conversion is the step that decides it: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, so 0·1 Å is 10⁻¹¹ m, and
getting that power wrong moves the answer by exactly one decade — which is why the options
are 10⁵, 10⁶, 10⁷ and 10⁸.
The result is the point of the question. Pinning an electron's position down to a tenth of an
ångström — a tenth of an atom's width — leaves its velocity uncertain by **5·79 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹**,
nearly **2 % of the speed of light**. The uncertainty is larger than any speed the electron
is likely to have, so its velocity is effectively unknown.
That is why the Bohr picture of an electron on a definite orbit with a definite speed had to
be abandoned for orbitals, which give only a probability of finding the electron.
∴ 5·79 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
